name: Cyclone Nargis (2008)
when: 27 April–3 May 2008; landfall about 12:00 UTC, 2 May
headline: An unusual eastward track took a rapidly intensifying cyclone straight into the low, crowded Irrawaddy Delta, where the surge ran about 40 km inland. The military government then restricted foreign aid for weeks.
numbers: 27 April–3 May 2008; landfall about 12:00 UTC, 2 May
84,537 dead and 53,836 missing (official post-disaster needs assessment)
Medium: contemporary official or survey estimate with known gaps
timeline: Forms in the central Bay of Bengal; named Nargis.
Turns almost due east toward Myanmar and intensifies rapidly.
Landfall in the Ayeyarwady Division at peak strength (about 215 km/h, 1-minute winds); the surge pushes about 40 km up the delta.
Passes just north of Yangon and dissipates near the Thai border.
The government accepts limited international aid; most aid workers are refused visas.
The junta holds its constitutional referendum, postponed to 24 May only in the worst-hit areas.
After meeting UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, the government opens access to aid workers.

The weather setup: Nargis turned nearly due east on 1 May and intensified rapidly over warm water just before reaching the coast, arriving at its strongest: a weak Category 4 equivalent.
What made it so deadly: The delta is flat, crowded with farming and fishing villages, and laced with channels that let the surge travel far inland. In Labutta Township state media reported 75% of buildings collapsed. India had warned Myanmar about 48 hours ahead, but there were no shelters and little evacuation.

The response compounded the disaster: the military government restricted visas and refused a US naval aid group, which left after weeks without delivering its supplies. A week after the storm only about one in ten people in need had received help. The feared second wave of deaths from disease did not materialise.
The death toll and why it is uncertain: The official post-disaster needs assessment gave 84,537 dead and 53,836 missing, a combined 138,373; the missing are presumed dead. Reports alleged the count stopped being updated at about 138,000, so the true toll may be higher. Damage was about US$10–15 billion, the costliest North Indian Ocean cyclone until Amphan in 2020.
